ARC: The Fall of Euija (655–660)

=== EPISODE 56: Exile (655)
Queen Satek, Euija’s mother, dies. Euija begins the traditional mourning period.
Three years of it, by the rite. For three years the king may not sit in judgement, may not sign, may not overturn. Everyone in Sabi knows exactly how long three years is, and exactly what can be done inside them.
The Queen was Satek. Her death removes the clan’s hand from the king’s sleeve, and the clan understands, before the funeral rites are finished, that the sleeve is now free.
The Satek clan begins to worry that Euija is about to exact revenge on them, especially his confidante — Hundred-Victories Gyebek.
They have watched him work. On the border, Gyebek earned his nickname mostly one way. He leaves the line to other men and goes looking for the general. His black horse, Gomanari, is the fastest thing on four legs in Samhan. Gyebek rides him flat along the neck like a thrown knife, the blade reversed along his forearm. The general sees a black shape where the field was empty. He starts to turn his horse, and does not finish turning. One cut on the pass. By the time the escort draws, the black horse is a speck on the far ridge. An army stands in a field with nobody left to tell it what to do.
eldersatek: He doesn’t ride at armies. / He rides at one man. / When the mourning’s over, whose house do you suppose that horse turns toward.
Gyebek has no clan. That is the whole problem. A man with a clan can be bargained with — you find out what his family wants and you give them some of it. A man with no clan wants only what the king wants, and there is nothing to buy.
They put him on a ship the way you put a problem past the horizon. The berth he leaves from is Satek water; the captain who will not meet his eyes holds a Yunbi winter contract. Even exile, in Baekje, has to borrow a clan’s harbour.
ministersatek: See him off cleanly. / If the orange island’s pilots gossip, let them gossip about weather — not about which house signed the sail.
So the two largest houses in Baekje meet, which has not happened in living memory except across a body.
They meet at night, at a monastery that belongs to neither of them, and each brings the same number of men, counted twice at the gate by both sides.
eldersatek: Lord Yunbi. How many generations have we been at this?
elderyunbi: Four. / Two of the three who died at the lantern festival last year were my nephews.
eldersatek: One of them was my grandson.
Neither of them apologises. Nobody expected it and it would have ended the meeting.
Halfway through the wine, a servant finds a second set of footprints behind the monastery screen — too small for the counted guards, too careful for a pilgrim. Yunbi’s man and Satek’s man look at each other and, for once, do not accuse. Someone is listening for a third house. Or for the king.
eldersatek: Spill the cups. / Tonight the doors matter more than the words.
elderyunbi: So why did you send for me tonight.
ministersatek: His Majesty has more than forty sons. / Where do you imagine he means to seat them.
elderyunbi: …In our chairs.
ministersatek: In the chairs of all eight houses.
It goes quiet. Outside, the two sets of men are standing apart in the courtyard, arranged by habit into the shape of a fight.
elderyunbi: We will destroy each other and lose everything. / …For how long.
eldersatek: As long as it takes. / After that we go back to the way we were.
elderyunbi: Agreed. / What gets removed first.
ministersatek: The one with no house.
They do not say his name at the table. Two houses that have not agreed on anything since before the capital moved agree, in under an hour, on one soldier with no family — and the agreement is written down nowhere, because agreements like that never are.
eldersatek: There is no price on that man.
ministersatek: Things without a price get removed.
They try the ordinary way first: they offer him a name. A real one, an old one, the eighth branch of a minor house, papers and a grave-line and ancestors. It is a serious offer and it is the only thing he has ever wanted.
gyebek: …I already have one.
eldersatek: The king made that one up.
gyebek: Yes. Which is why it is owed to someone.
Hundred-Victories narrowly escapes an assassination attempt, and begins to take security measures.
The arrow comes through a tent wall at the Ungjin drill ground and takes the man standing next to him, who was taller. Nobody is ever charged. The fletching is Baekje army issue, which narrows it to about nine thousand people, which is the point of using it.
He stops eating food he has not watched being cooked. He sleeps in a different room each night, which the ministers immediately report to the regency as the behaviour of a man planning something.
seongchung: General. You should be away from here. / Half a year. Until His Majesty is out of mourning.
gyebek: …I don’t run.
seongchung: Which is exactly how they win.
The order comes down while the king is still in mourning and cannot countermand it. Hundred-Victories Gyebek is put on a boat.
Nine, by then. Gyebek had been counting for years, quietly, the way you keep an eye on a leak.
To worship your own kind blindly is foolish; to hate your own kind blindly is more foolish still.
The truce holds exactly as long as it needs to. Four generations of blood, suspended for the length of one signature, and both houses will go back to burning each other’s carts before the year is out.
Gyebek is summoned to the hall and told to kneel, and the order is read out over his head.
The order is genuine. That is the craftsmanship of it. It bears the royal seal, because a king in mourning leaves his seal with the Assembly so that the country does not stop, and the Assembly has had it for four months.
It is read with the king’s formula and the king’s seal — but not by the king. Minister Satek holds the Assembly’s borrowed stamp; the voice in the hall is the Premier’s.
ministersatek: The seal is set. / Minister Satek — I read this in the Assembly’s name. / Gyebek is hereby sent into exile!
chunbok: …It is His Majesty’s will.
Remember the young Satek who just called it His Majesty’s will. He will say worse things in His Majesty’s name, later, to a much bigger king.
gyebek: …What did you say?
He is put on the boat the same afternoon. Satek water at the berth; a Yunbi winter contract in the captain’s sleeve. Even exile borrows a clan harbour.
He wakes on a beach with sand in his teeth and no idea how many days it has been. The not-knowing is worse than the beach.
gyebek: How many days.
yuridora: Ah. Not one for greetings, then.
gyebek: …How many days.
yuridora: Eleven. Better?
It is better. Visibly. The islanders will spend five years noticing that this man is calmed by numbers and unsettled by almost everything else.
yuridora: Your name?
gyebek: I am called Gyebek.
yuridora: What? A man named turtle?
gyebek: No. Gye is the stone step, and baek is the eldest.
yuridora: …It was a joke.
gyebek: …Ah.
He says ah the way another man would say I will write that down. It would be a mistake to read the pause as slowness; somewhere behind those eyes, a ledger has just gained a line.
A man who cannot hear a joke will hear an order perfectly. Be careful what you give him.
Euija completes his mourning period — and discovers that Gyebek has been exiled. Not by his hand. By the clans. By Minister Satek reading a sealed order while the king was barred from countermanding it.
euija: Who. / Who used my seal — / Who took my man —
ministersatek: Your Majesty… the Assembly— / In mourning the council—
euija: Minister Satek! / I swear I’ll just— overturn the whole lot of them like Gesomun did!! / You put my man on a boat? You used my mourning as a gap?
There is nothing theatrical in the fury. It is the sound a king makes on learning that three years of rite turned him into a stamp — and that the stamp signed away the one soldier who never asked him for a clan chair.
## Black Rock
He trains at the same hour on the same slab of lava on the eastern shore, and when the tide takes that slab he waits for the tide rather than use another one.
yuridora: The next rock is the same.
gyebek: It is not the same.
The rock is porous and cruel and nothing like a drill ground. You cannot plant a foot on it twice in the same place. Two seasons of it and he no longer needs to know where his feet are.
haenyeo: You don’t hold the breath. You push it out with singing.
gyebek: …I cannot sing.
haenyeo: Nobody cannot. There are only people who don’t.
The village children learn the count of his drills before they learn his name, and stand on the rocks doing it badly behind him, and he does not once turn round to stop them, because stopping would be an interruption and he does not interrupt.
A man who cannot vary anything will be unbeatable on the ground he chose, and helpless on any other. Give him the choosing.
## Five Thousand
He is asked, once, why he counts everything, and he answers honestly, which is the only way he has ever answered anything.
gyebek: Numbers do not lie to me.
yuridora: And people do?
gyebek: People are not trying to. / I simply do not follow them. / I have never learned to read a face.
yuridora: Then how did you survive twenty years at a court?
gyebek: I trusted one man.
The island considers this the saddest sentence anybody has said on it, and nobody explains to him why they have all gone quiet, and he does not ask, because he has not noticed.
?: (Tamla fisher, laughing) / Hundred-Victories, they call him on the mainland — and here he counts oranges like they might desert.
He drills in units of five hundred. Four years from now he will take ten of those units to a field and leave the rest behind. The count is already in his mouth.
Give a literal man one person to trust and you have not given him a friend. You have given him a hinge.
First night on the island. A fire, two cups, and a storyteller who never asks permission. “Sit or don’t. Once there were two suns…”

=== EPISODE 57: Heaven–Earth King (태초) [flashback]
Told on the first night, before he has agreed to listen to anything. Yuri Dora has a fire going, two cups, and no plan to ask permission.
yuridora: I’ll start at the beginning. / Sit or don’t.
Gyebek stays standing by the door. Yuri Dora starts anyway.
In the beginning there were two suns and two moons. By day people dropped in the fields with their hoes still in their hands; by night they froze in their own doorways. Nobody ever had a decent night’s sleep or a decent harvest, and the old died faster than anyone could bury them.
Above all of it sat Heaven–Earth King, who ran the living and the dead out of one office and therefore never went home. One night he fell asleep at the desk anyway, and dreamed he was eating: one sun, one moon, swallowed whole, one of each.
heavenearthking: ……Huh. / One each. / I ate one of each. / Ha— that’s a son. Someone’s going to shoot those down.
He comes down to the world to find the mother of that dream, and finds her in the poorest house on the road: a girl the village calls the Lady of Wisdom, a hearth with no fire in it, and a rice jar she does not open in front of guests.
chongmyeong: Who are you.
heavenearthking: Someone passing. / A hungry one.
chongmyeong: ……Sit, then.
She goes round the back and lifts the lid of the jar. The bottom of it looks up at her. She puts the lid back as if that might help, ties up her hair, and walks across the road.
Across the road lives Sumyung Jangja, who is rich the way a flood is wet. He has nine storehouses, a horse that kicks beggars, a dog that bites whatever the horse misses, and a rice measure that comes out a little smaller when he lends and a little larger when he collects.
chongmyeong: Lend me one measure of rice. / I have a guest.
sumyeongjangja: One measure. / Two when you pay it back. / A guest? Anyone who’d come to your house, I can guess.
chongmyeong: Two, then.
He fills the measure himself, with his back to her.
She washes it nine times at the well and spends the last of her firewood on it. The king takes the first spoonful. Something in his mouth grinds.
heavenearthking: …… / Your rice has a bit of bite to it.
chongmyeong: ……It’s sand. / I washed it nine times.
heavenearthking: Who gave it to you.
chongmyeong: The house across the road. / I said I’d pay back two.
heavenearthking: Two. / One measure with sand in it, for two. / ……Eat. Eat all of it. I’m stepping out for a minute.
Sumyung Jangja is counting his storehouses, which is how he prays, when the sky over the ninth one goes black at noon. The horse will not kick. The dog gets under the porch.
sumyeongjangja: Who’s there. / There’s nobody under heaven who can touch me.
heavenearthking: That’s why I came from above.
sumyeongjangja: ……W-what is it you want. / Rice? If it’s rice— two measures, no, ten, the whole storehouse—
heavenearthking: Without the sand?
The floor of the ninth storehouse opens. The richest man in the world goes down through it, past the dirt and past the dark, into the place under everything where the measures are honest. He is the first one there. He will not be lonely for long.
He goes back across the road. He stays until the day the calendar allows, and the morning after, he is already tying his sleeves.
chongmyeong: You’re going?
heavenearthking: Lots of work upstairs. / There are two suns, remember.
heavenearthking: Two sons. The first one out is Daebyeol, the second one Sobyeol. / When they turn fifteen, have them plant these.
Two gourd seeds in her palm, and half of a wooden comb. The other half goes into his sleeve.
chongmyeong: ……Fifteen years.
heavenearthking: …… / Thanks for the rice.
She has twins. The elder comes out quiet and looks at everything. The younger comes out already complaining. They grow up under two suns and two moons, and get asked whose sons they are in every yard in the village.
sobyeol: Mom. Who’s our father. / The other kids are at it again.
daebyeol: Leave it. Mom’s tired.
chongmyeong: ……When you’re fifteen.
At fifteen she puts the seeds in their hands and the half comb in the elder’s. They plant them by the wall at dusk. By morning the vine has gone past the roof, past the clouds, and out of sight.
chongmyeong: Climb. / All the way up.
sobyeol: What about you?
chongmyeong: I’ll be here. I’ll have rice on.
Sobyeol gets to the top first and pretends he wasn’t racing. The man at the top of the vine holds out his hand without getting up.
heavenearthking: The comb.
Daebyeol puts the half in his palm. The king takes the other half out of his sleeve, where it has been for fifteen years, and fits them. The teeth close.
heavenearthking: ……Fits.
sobyeol: You never came down. Not once.
heavenearthking: ……There were two suns.
He has a thousand geun of iron melted down into two bows and two arrows, heavy enough that nobody but a son of his could draw them, and walks the boys to the edge of the sky.
heavenearthking: Two suns, two moons. / Two of each over your mother’s roof for fifteen years. / One each.
Daebyeol takes the sun at noon. He breathes out once and lets go, and the second sun breaks like a plate. Its pieces scatter east and stay there as stars. At midnight Sobyeol draws on the second moon and hits it square, and its pieces go west.
sobyeol: Brother. Got it in one. / You saw?
daebyeol: I saw.
In the morning people go out to the fields and do not fall down. That night they sleep. Nobody thanks anyone, because nobody knows who to thank.
heavenearthking: Done. The world’s yours. / The living side and the dead side. You two decide who takes which. / I’m not deciding. Whoever I pick always comes back to argue. / I’m resting.
They decide it the way brothers decide things. Daebyeol proposes riddles, which suits the one who knows the answers.
daebyeol: Which trees keep their leaves all their lives, and which ones drop them?
sobyeol: Solid ones keep them. Hollow ones drop them.
daebyeol: Poor little brother, don’t talk about what you don’t know. / Bamboo and reeds are hollow at every joint, and they keep their leaves.
sobyeol: ……Another.
daebyeol: Why is the grass short on the hill and long down in the hollow?
sobyeol: Spring rain washes the hill’s dirt down into the hollow.
daebyeol: Then why is the hair on your head long and the hair on your feet short?
sobyeol: …… / That one’s cheating.
Two for two. Their father, who said he would not decide anything, leans over the edge of his rest and drops two flower seeds between them.
heavenearthking: Flowers. / Whoever grows the better one gets the living side. / ……That’s me done interfering.
They plant them in two silver basins and sit up with them. Daebyeol’s flower comes up green and keeps coming, and by the third evening it has opened. Sobyeol’s comes up yellow and leans.
sobyeol: Let’s sleep, Brother. / We’ll look in the morning. See whose did better.
daebyeol: All right.
Daebyeol sleeps the way honest men sleep, all the way down. Sobyeol lies on his side and counts his brother’s breathing up to a hundred. Then he gets up, trades the basins, and lies down again in the same shape, so his brother will wake first.
sobyeol: ……Brother! Wake up! / Look, it’s mine!
Daebyeol looks at the open flower in front of his brother, the one he watered for three days. He looks at the yellow one by his own hand.
daebyeol: …… / Yes. Your flower did well.
He gets up and brushes the soil off his knees.
daebyeol: Brother, countless people live in the mortal world. Among them are thieves and swindlers. To govern them well you need strength and wisdom — but above all, a true heart. So govern them, and make a beautiful, peaceful world.
He is already walking toward the dark edge when he says the rest, and he does not turn round.
daebyeol: But, little brother. You took it with a stolen flower. / The living world will have plenty of murder, plenty of treason, plenty of thieves, and plenty of people reaching for other people’s wives and husbands. / The law down below will run clear.
sobyeol: ……Brother! / Brother, that’s—
Big Star goes down. Little Star keeps the warm side.
It goes the way his brother said, and worse, because Sobyeol had never thought about the parts he didn’t want. The trees still talk. So do the birds, the cattle and the stones, mostly about him. When a mother calls her son’s name at dusk a ghost answers too, and the living and the dead walk the same roads in the same clothes, and nobody can tell which is which.
sobyeol: Brother. / Brother, help me, just this once. / The trees talk. The ghosts answer. I can’t tell who’s a man and who’s a ghost.
Big Star comes up. He scatters five measures of pine-bark powder over the world, and the trees and the birds and the cattle go quiet and have stayed quiet since. Then he hangs a scale from the sky.
daebyeol: Line up. / A hundred geun or more, you stay up here. / Less, you come with me.
sobyeol: ……And the thieves? The ones who kill people?
daebyeol: Those are your flower.
He goes back down with the light ones following him in a long quiet line. Since then the dead weigh less than the living, the law below runs clear, and the law up here belongs to Little Star. Under Big Star, Yumla judges, and the measures are honest.
The fire has gone low. Gyebek sat down at some point and does not remember when.
gyebek: ……Did the brother know. That the flowers were switched.
yuridora: He knew.
gyebek: And he gave it up anyway.
yuridora: He did. And he went down. / Down there is the dead world, up here the living. There’s a flower field out at the western end, and above all of it, old Lord Hwanin. / Three Realms, all told. Tonight you only need the two.
gyebek: ……Rice with sand in it.
yuridora: Hm?
gyebek: Nothing.
It is the first story on the island he does not inspect.
The world was not given to the better brother. Stop waiting for it to behave as if it was.
The next night he hides on a roof. She tells it anyway. One woman made this island, and she was enormous…!

=== EPISODE 58: Sulmun (태초) [flashback]
The next story is told to him on a roof, because he is on a roof, mending it, and Yuri Dora has decided that a man who will not sit down can still listen.
yuridora: One woman made this island. Sulmun.
Before the island there is a woman, and she is enormous. Sulmun, the Great Lady. The sea comes to her knee. She scoops the seabed up in her apron and piles it in one place until it stands high enough to lean on, and that is Mount Halla.
gyebek: Was there a hole in the apron.
yuridora: …How did you know that?
gyebek: You said there are three hundred and sixty-eight hills. / If it were poured in one place there would be one.
Yuri Dora looks at him for a while.
yuridora: You do not listen to a story. You inspect it.
gyebek: …Yes.
She had five hundred sons. In a famine she set a cauldron of porridge to boil for them, and slipped, and did not come out. The sons ate. It was the best they had ever tasted, and they said so, and then the youngest reached the bottom and found his mother’s bones.
The youngest walked into the sea and would not turn round, and stands there yet as a single rock off the shore. The other four hundred and ninety-nine went up the mountain and wept until they were stone. You can go and count them. Nobody has ever got the same number twice.
She asked the islanders for one thing: clothes her size, a hundred rolls of silk, and she would lay a bridge to the mainland. They found ninety-nine. The collar was never finished. Neither was the bridge.
gyebek: They were one roll short.
yuridora: They were.
gyebek: …That is the worst amount to be short by.
The bridge was not lost to the sea. It was lost to the last one per cent.
Three princes climb out of the ground. “Not from an egg,” the island insists. Then a box drifts in from the sea…!

=== EPISODE 59: Three Princes (태초) [flashback]
This is the story of the kingdom of Tamla.
[diagram tamla-princes]
Long after the Great Lady’s stone sons, three divine princes named Yang, Go and Bu climb out of a hole in the ground.
yuridora: Not from an egg. / This island says that with feeling.
yang_tamla: We divide the land. By arrow.
go_tamla: Shorter than talk. Good.
bu_tamla: I aim east.
They each shoot an arrow and rule over each piece of the island.
One day a box drifts from the East Sea — a messenger and three princesses inside.
yang_tamla: Marriage. Debate later.
They marry the three princesses at a pond. The box holds calves, foals, and the five grains — which is how Tamla learns to farm, and how Tamla learns that anything worth having tends to arrive by sea in a container.
Ever since, the island has sent Baekje oranges and, when asked, men.
Ordinary Tamla does not play the mainland’s endless status games. A diver offers Gyebek grilled fish before she asks which Baekje office ruined him. A boy corrects his orange-peeling and laughs when he fails. Kindness here is not strategy. That, more than the stories, is what keeps him five years.
haenyeo: Eat. / You look like a man who was promoted by being useful and punished for the same crime. That joke is how Little Star runs the living world.
gyebek: …That is an exact sentence.
haenyeo: We have those. We just don’t put them on banners.
## Baekjuto and Socheon-guk
Told while he is stacking oranges badly, which Yuri Dora treats as invitation.
yuridora: The hunting god married the farming goddess. / She gave him an ox to plough with—
gyebek: He ate it.
yuridora: …Have you heard this one?
gyebek: No. But he is a hunter.
baekjuto: You ate the ox. The one I gave you to plough with. The whole ox?
socheonguk: …I also ate someone else’s.
They separated. It is the first divorce in the record, the grounds are livestock, and the islanders tell it as a comedy because it is one.
Their son kicked his father in the chest at three years old. So they put the boy in an iron chest, locked it, and set it on the water.
It drifted for years and washed up in a foreign country, and the boy came out of it a warrior, and won that country’s wars, and married its princess. And then he came home.
gyebek: …Tell that part again.
yuridora: Which part.
gyebek: The part where he comes home.
yuridora: He came home and became the god of his own land. / The god the ones who threw him out have to bow to.
The sea does not decide what a man is. It only decides how long he waits to be it.
“Tomorrow’s isn’t a kind one, Turtle.” A serpent in a cave. A woman from the rock. A man who looks back…!

=== EPISODE 60: Stone Lady (태초) [flashback]
yuridora: Today’s is not a kind one.
gyebek: That is acceptable.
There is Kangrim — but the island does not tell his full story until last. For now it is enough to know he comes for you, and that a crow once ruined his schedule.
gyebek: …Would it be better to know.
yuridora: For you it would.
There is the serpent in the cave at Gimnyeong that took a girl a year until a young magistrate went in and killed it, and was told on the way out not to look back, and looked back.
gyebek: Why did he look back.
yuridora: To check that he had won.
There is Sanbangduk, who came down out of the rock to love a poor man.
sanbangdeok: I came out of the rock… / and when I hold your hand I don’t feel like stone.
herald: Then don’t let go. / Whatever the official says.
They don’t let go — until the official has the husband killed to take her. She walks back into the cliff. The spring inside it has not stopped since.
gyebek: The official wanted her. The world wanted the wrong thing. / So she went back into the rock. / …Sometimes the rock looks cleaner.
yuridora: Cleaner is not the same as finished. / Stone stays. It does not ride.
gyebek: Do all the stories on this island end badly.
yuridora: No. They all end as stone. / That’s not the same as badly. Stone stays.
Do not turn round to confirm the victory. The looking is what collects the price.
## Gameunjang
Told at a well, while he is fixing the rope.
yuridora: A rich man had three daughters. He asked them whose luck they lived on.
yuridora: The elder two said his. The youngest said her own navel-string. / So she was thrown out.
gyebek: If she had lied she could have stayed.
yuridora: …Yes. She could have.
She walked until she found three brothers digging yams and married the youngest, the only one who greeted her. In the spoil he had been throwing away as stones, she found gold.
Her parents lost everything and went blind. Years later she held a beggars’ feast that lasted three days, and served two old blind beggars herself, and said her name, and their eyes opened.
gyebek: …So the child they threw away was the luck.
yuridora: No. The luck was always hers. / It was the ones who threw her out who went blind.
He does not answer that one. He finishes the rope, and tests it eleven times.
Cast out what carries your fortune and you will not see it go. That is what blindness is for.
Heaven sends for a man to keep its flower field. He leaves his pregnant wife to wait. He forgets to say how long…!

=== EPISODE 61: Gardener (태초) [flashback]
Told in the orange grove, in the hour after the picking, when Gyebek has finally been persuaded to sit on a basket.
yuridora: There was a man called Sara Doryeong. Heaven sent for him to keep its flower field in the west. / His wife was carrying. She couldn’t walk as fast as heaven wanted, so he left her at a rich man’s house to wait.
gyebek: How long was she to wait.
yuridora: He didn’t say. / That’s the first mistake. Count it if you like.
The rich man wanted her. Wonganghami said no, and went on saying no for fifteen years, through every kind of work a rich man can find for a servant who says no. Her son was born in that house and grew up a servant in it. His name was Hallakgungi.
yuridora: When he was old enough she told him where his father was. He went west that night. / And the rich man, when he found the boy gone, killed the mother instead and threw her into a bamboo grove.
gyebek: …She knew he would.
yuridora: She knew. / She told him anyway.
Hallakgungi found the flower field at the far end of the west, where the living maps run out, and his father at the gate of it. Sara Doryeong took him down the rows. Here, the flowers that put back bone, and flesh, and blood, and breath, and the soul last of all. Over there, the flowers that laugh a man to death, and the ones that make a house fight itself, and at the end of the row the one that ends a line altogether.
gyebek: Which did he take.
yuridora: Both rows. / He went back to that rich man’s house and held a little party. Laughing flower, fighting flower, and the last one. Then he went to the bamboo grove and found his mother’s bones, and put her back together in order. Bone, flesh, blood, breath, soul.
gyebek: In order. / …Good.
Afterwards the son took the flower field over from his father and keeps it still. The island calls him the Gardener when it does not want to say his name, which is most of the time. The flowers that bring you back and the flowers that end you grow in the same rows, and he is the only one who knows which is which in the dark.
gyebek: Did the father go home with them.
yuridora: No. He kept the gate till the boy was ready for it. / …You ask the right questions in the wrong places, Turtle.
The flower that brings back and the flower that ends grow in the same row. Learn which is which before you need them.
## Jacheongbi
Told in the rain, in a doorway, which is the only time anyone gets him to stand still.
yuridora: Jacheongbi wanted to study beside a boy from the sky. / Women were not allowed in the room, so she cut her hair and put on a man’s clothes.
gyebek: Did she break the rule.
yuridora: No. The rule never said a woman could not wear a man’s clothes.
gyebek: …Ah.
That one he likes. That one he asks to hear twice.
Three years at the same desk. She beat him at everything and let him believe it was close. On the last night at the parting stream she washed upstream of him and told him to look.
jacheongbi: Three years at the same table — eating, sleeping, reading — and you notice now?
mundoryeong: …I had no eyes.
jacheongbi: You have them now. / …Will you only look? / After three years of holding back.
mundoryeong: I was not holding back. / I did not know. / Now that I do… my breath is rough.
jacheongbi: Then stay rough. / Touch my hair. / The hair I cut short for you.
They killed him for it. Heaven does not care for that sort of marriage. So she walked west — past every gate — into the Western Flower Field.
sara: Father retired. / This gate answers to Hallakgungi now. / What are you looking for.
jacheongbi: The resurrection flower. / The one that puts bones back together.
sara: Don’t touch the stem wrong. / Five — bone, flesh, blood, breath, soul. / Pick them out of order and even the living wilt.
jacheongbi: I’ll pick them in order.
She took what she needed, put Mun Doryeong back together bone by bone, and brought the five grains down to Tamla.
gyebek: …Can the dead be fetched back.
yuridora: In stories.
gyebek: …I see.
The rule is smaller than you think, and the door is usually in the wording. Read it again.
The island keeps one story for last. It is about the one who comes for you, and the crow that lost his book…!

=== EPISODE 62: Kangrim (태초) [flashback]
The island keeps one story for last. After it, every ending on the mainland has a broken clock already running.
yuridora: Now the last one. / Kangrim. / Heaven did not send him.
A magistrate named Kimchi had a murder he could not try. Three brothers were killed for their silk and sunk in a pond. They came back as three flowers on the water. Burned, they became three beads. A woman swallowed them and bore three sons. The sons came home from the exams and died in one bow. Their mother would not stop writing petitions. So Kimchi sent his strongest man, Kangrim, to bring King Yumla up and close the case.
gyebek: …He sent a living man to arrest the judge of the dead.
yuridora: He did.
His wife kept the gate-god and the kitchen-god fed, so they put him on the road. At the last pond he shut his eyes and jumped, and stood up at the underworld gate. Someone was already walking that road with a red book. Haewonmek, the oldest fetch there is. Kangrim asked the way. Haewonmek pointed, and kept walking. Kangrim waited, and addressed King Yumla with court courtesy.
kangrim: Your Majesty. The living court requests you. / There is a case. Living law cannot close it.
yumla: Go home. / I will come at the hour I name.
He came. The pond dried. The bones came up. The three brothers went home to their parents. The couple who had killed them did not. Yumla keeps the sentence. Then he turned to the magistrate and asked to borrow the man who had fetched him.
yumla: Lend me that man. I still have errands.
yuridora: The magistrate refused. He did not believe in a soul. / So they split him. The magistrate kept the body. Yumla took the soul.
That is how Kangrim died upstairs and woke as a chasa. The living official kept the half he could see. Death kept the other half.
gyebek: …They divided a man.
yuridora: They both wanted him.
Yumla then put in his hands a ledger that told each living person their hour — eighty, and in order, the old before the young. On the way down Kangrim trusted it to a crow. The crow set the book on a wall to eat at a slaughter-field. A snake swallowed the writing. Caught, the crow cried a new rule so the blame would not sit on one bird: parents after children, children after parents. Since then the hour does not come in a just order.
One errand was left. A man called Dongbangsak had lived three thousand years and would not come. Kangrim sat in a stream washing charcoal. Dongbangsak stopped. He had never, in all that time, heard of washing charcoal white. Kangrim took him by the sleeve. Only then did Yumla seat him as the one who comes for everyone else. That is why he asks a question at the threshold. Not for the sentence — Yumla keeps the sentence. A scrambled list still deserves accurate last words.
kangrim: I do not punish. / I collect — for His Majesty. / Since the list was scrambled, nobody knows the hour until I am already in the room.
gyebek: …Then a man can die before his king, and the book still opens.
yuridora: The book went wrong on the road. The walk did not. / That is the key.
The warrant said die in order. A crow lost it. You do not get a fair hour. You still get the door.
Why does an orange island take Baekje’s exiles at all? Because once, long ago, it forgot to send the oranges…!

=== EPISODE 63: Tribute (498) [flashback]
Tamla stops sending tribute. Rebellion would at least have been legible; this is closer to forgetting, which a large kingdom finds harder to forgive.
Baekje’s king marches an army to the southern harbour and stops. He lets the news cross the water on its own. It gets there faster than he would have.
Tamla apologises. Baekje accepts. Nobody is killed, everybody is satisfied, and the oranges resume. For a hundred and fifty years, that is the whole relationship.
So when Baekje needs somewhere to put a man it cannot kill, there is an island, and the island owes it a favour.
Meanwhile, in Sabi, Euija calls the Assembly. He has a smile, a speech, and a proclamation printed before anyone sat down…!

=== EPISODE 64: Coup (655)
He calls the assembly the way a gambler calls a final hand — smiling, sleeves perfect, already knowing which tiles he slipped into the set.
Euija calls a session of the Ministers’ Assembly at Deer Rock. The rock is dry. Someone forgot the brine, or remembered it and chose not to.
euija: Beloved people. / As Eraha, I appeal to you with a heart that spits blood.
euija: To protect Baekje from the threat of Silla, / to eradicate in one stroke the shameless pro-Tang anti-state forces that plunder our people’s freedom and happiness, / and to safeguard the free order of this country — / I hereby declare emergency martial law.
euija: Through this emergency martial law, I will rebuild and protect Baekje, which is falling into the abyss of national ruin. / To that end I will absolutely eradicate the anti-state forces — the main culprits of national ruin — who have habitually engaged in heinous acts up till now.
euija: This is an inevitable measure to guarantee the people’s freedom and safety, and the continuity of the nation, against anti-state forces that bid to overthrow the system — / so that we may pass on a proper country to future generations. / I will eradicate the anti-state forces and normalize the nation in the shortest possible time.
euija: Due to this declaration, there may be some inconveniences for the good people who have believed in and followed the lawful order of this country. / We will strive to minimize such inconveniences. / This measure is inevitable for the perpetuity of Baekje, / and there is no change in our foreign stance toward Wa, Tang, or any neighbour.
euija: As Eraha, I earnestly appeal to the people. / I place my trust solely in you, and I will devote body and life to protecting Baekje. / Please trust me.
He has a script ready: dissolve the Assembly, seat his own blood, call the pause a rescue. The clans stare. He expected applause. The room stays quiet.
chunbok: King Onjo preserve us — he’s lost his mind… / Also he printed the proclamation before the session. I can smell the ink. / The characters for “in one stroke” are still wet.
euija: This is temporary. / Temporary is how permanent things begin when you are afraid to say permanent.
Then he unrolls a second scroll — shorter, denser, the kind of law that fits on one sheet because the power is in what it erases. The clerks name it before he does: the Law to Remedy the Distress of the People and the Country.
euija: In addition to the procedure prescribed by the Assembly, / laws of Baekje may also be enacted by the Eraha’s command. / Such laws may deviate from the old custom — insofar as the Assembly as such is not abolished.
euija: The throne will make use of this authorization only insofar as it is essential for carrying out vitally necessary measures. / The existence of the Assembly is not endangered. The Premier’s chair remains undisturbed. / The rights of the temples will not be curtailed.
ministersatek: Your Majesty. That is… a law for emptying the Assembly. / It keeps the name. It changes the people.
euija: If the name remains, the country remains. / If the people remain, the people eat the country. / May you now choose for yourselves — peace, or war.
Nobody chooses war out loud. Choosing peace means raising a sleeve for the scroll. The rock does not sweat. The sleeves go up anyway — some of them already paid, some of them already afraid, some of them already his sons waiting in the corridor.
Euija names forty-one of his own sons to the Assembly, firing every single existing member. Eight houses spent four generations sharpening tricks on each other. Marriages. Roads. Clerks planted in rival counting-rooms. In one morning the king clears the board. He simply changes the pieces. By noon nobody has an answer.
Forty-one sons need forty-one seats. None goes to the Ye family. They have held Bear Fortress for four generations and never once been asked to court. Ye Sikjin reads the list at home, twice. Then he puts it in a drawer.
Then he hands out the quiet money that really runs Baekje. Harbour warehouses. River pilot fees. The stamp a ship needs before it sails east. The martial law was the noise. The stamps are what change.
He cannot do what Yeon did. Baekje would not forgive it, and more to the point, he would not. He does not need a banquet. He needs a majority that looks like kinship.
The clans try to rally — Satek calling in four generations of favors, the old Assembly men lining up behind them. But a face-off only works if you know your opponent’s style, and Euija has spent twenty years teaching them his. They line up for a duel. He has already changed who is sitting.
He’s recruited Satek Chunbok, one of the clan’s own young men, as his eyes inside their hall — the oldest technique in the book, turned on the house that wrote the book.
He’s also recruited the other clans — the houses Satek had crowded out of the light, every one of them delighted to lend the king a blade for this particular duel.
euija: You too! You’re a Satek lackey, aren’t you??!!
Satek Chunbok is named Premier. His own clan finds out with everyone else. The Enabling Law did not abolish the chair. It only changed who sits in it.
courtmaid: Your Majesty. How many did you dismiss today? / …And how many of us will you keep.
euija: All of them. / You… I keep.
courtmaid: …How frightening. / And yet — that kind of Majesty… feels nearer.
euija: …What was your name again.
courtmaid: I don’t have one yet. / Make me one tonight. / As you did for General Gyebek — take your time.
Eleven of them by nightfall.
gaozong: So… Baekje? What of Baekje—
chunbok: Do not trouble yourself over Baekje.
gaozong: ?
chunbok: Baekje will fall on its own. / Where blood ties are strong, the state grows weak. / The Baekje clans love a family feud — they will envy each other into ruin.
gaozong: Then why am I needed at all?
chunbok: However weak it is, it still needs one shock. / Say the Tang army is coming — the rumour alone will tip the country’s spirit.
He beat eight houses in one morning. Now he can’t sleep. In his dreams, somebody keeps counting…?

=== EPISODE 65: Descent (656)
## Nightmares
He starts dreaming about the Rock of Politics. In the dream it is dry, and he is rubbing it with brine, and the brine will not stay. Every time he lifts the cloth the stone is dry again, and the eight elders are standing round it waiting for it to sweat.
Some nights it is the white deer, come back out of the dark it was kept in, and too big for the hunting ground. Some nights it is a boat on the water with a man sitting very straight in the stern, not rowing, counting.
euija: (waking, to the dark) Who’s counting? / …Who’s there. Light. Somebody bring a light!
courtmaid: Majesty. It’s only us. / …You were saying numbers again.
euija: Wine. / No. Don’t water it. I can tell when you water it.
Euija becomes increasingly paranoid about the aftershock of his purge. He beat eight houses in a single morning, and now he lives inside the winner’s arithmetic: eight grudges, forty-one sons, and not one loyalty left that he did not create by decree.
Among the first sent away, by decree this time, is Heungsu. He had the bad manners to say the purge would finish what Silla could not. Euija calls it a temporary posting. The court knows better. The paper names a county far to the south. Packed earth. A magistrate’s hut with a doorpost for a ring.
Gomamiji is a posting, not a retirement. He sits on the threshold until the dust on the hem looks like the hem. The hollow ring leans on the timber. Nobody from Sabi writes.
He stops holding court. The wine comes earlier each day, and then it stops being tied to the day at all.
Hundreds, by now. Nobody keeps the roll. They no longer have separate duties — only who pours, who steadies his wrist, who is still there when the wine runs out, and who is bold enough to speak while his mouth is busy elsewhere.
The hems keep time better than the roll. A pour, a step, a kneel — the long court silk opens, and he watches that before he watches the wine.
The feast is no longer a feast. Robes open. Knees find laps. He is half-undressed and does not bother to hide what the wine has done to him. The maids show him their bodies the way other courts show tribute.
The stories say three thousand. The room is not that. It is still too many — a harem so packed the lamp never finds a wall. They kneel in ranks. They loosen the silk. They climb into his lap two at a time. He does not hide what the wine has done; the dark trousers tell it first.
The hall is Sabi: vermilion columns, yellow wood, lamps on a wet floor. They fill it. They hike the silk. They turn their backs and laugh. They pour bent at the waist. They crowd a column. Ribbons come undone. They toast until the lamps blur. They compete to be seen.
A hand finds the silk at her own lap. Fingers rest on an inner thigh. One knee up. A twist. They show off for him.
Jackets hang off the shoulders. The chima rides low. The robe hangs open.
The headband is gone. The robe hangs off. They hike the silk to the hip. Inner thighs face him. A hem lifts. A maid finds his lap. His mouth finds the silk.
They hike it as high as it will go. Two of them hike together. They sit with knees up. One knee high. She pulls the silk up. He looks up the silk. His mouth is at her hip. The robe hangs wider.
They hike it to the last fold of silk. His mouth is along a thigh. The robe is open to the navel. Her hand on the silk at her lap. Jeogori slipping off the shoulders.
The party does not sit still. Wine-wet silk clinging. His hands on her thighs. They sit with both knees up. She twists at the waist. One of them, both knees up in his lap.
Moonlight through the lattice. One lamp from the side. Over her shoulder. On the night veranda. She pours clear wine down the silk. They laugh into the lamp.
Rain on the night veranda. A shaft of lamp in the dark. They take the night corridor. Moon on one side of his face.
She looks back, hip out. His hand finds the silk at her waist. The S-curve of a hip is the whole argument of the hall. Less clothes. More lamp. The robe hangs open. The jeogori does not stay on the shoulder.
His face finds a hip. He buries himself between them. He presses into the wet silk at her back. He goes face-first into the silk. An untied goreum. They gasp and laugh in his face.
courtmaid: Your Majesty. You said that yesterday, and again today. / …With the same breath on us. / The same teeth… at our collarbones.
euija: Was it good? / Or… was it a good night.
courtmaid: …It was, yesterday. / The body still remembers. / Even if Your Majesty says stop… the hips answer first.
courtmaid: Your Majesty. Tell us about when you were young. / Before you… undo anything. / No — / While you undo it. / One word per knot.
euija: …What is it you want to know.
courtmaid: They say you have more than fifty sons. / Samsin must keep a whole ledger just for Your Majesty. The kitchens have a wager going on how. / Nightly.
euija: …That was the thirtieth Eraha. My father.
courtmaid: Ah. Then Your Majesty still has room to work with. / We can testify to it.
courtmaid: We knew already, in fairness. / Asking was only manners.
He laughs for the first time in four months. It is the last recorded instance.
Somewhere in the third year he stops going out to the hall, and some time after that they stop sending for him. The distance between those two things is the rest of the reign.
chunbok: Your Majesty…
chunbok: Would it not be best to bring back General Gyebek?
euija: That… who? / You there! Bring more wine!
nation-baekje: Ahh~~ over here, Your Majesty~~
courtmaid: Your Majesty. The ministers are waiting outside.
euija: …Let them wait.
courtmaid: Until when?
euija: …
He does not answer. After a while the question stops being asked, and after a while longer the ministers stop coming to the door. He notices none of it, and it is the first thing in his life he has not arranged on purpose.
Seongchung comes while the wine is still being poured. He does not wait for a gap. The ring at his hip catches the lamp when he steps — a hollow circle, nothing poetic, just the office blade of a man who used to read tides.
seongchung: Your Majesty. Open court. / Today.
euija: We opened it. / With the cup.
seongchung: There is a tide. / If you miss it—
He does not finish. The king is already angry. The belt comes off in the aisle. After that, nobody else tries to speak.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 16 (656), third month] The king was angry and imprisoned him. After that, there was no one who dared to speak.
Seongchung starves in a cell within earshot of the feast. The ring hangs on the post. With the last of his ink he leaves the king one piece of paper.
In the cell where he starved, Kangrim reads his name three times — Seongchung. Seongchung. Seongchung. — loud enough for the feast next door to hear, or not hear.
kangrim: Councillor Seongchung. / You chose the cell over silence. Was that loyalty to the king — or loyalty to being right?
seongchung: …Being right is the only loyalty left when a king stops listening. / The paper is for him. Not for you.
kangrim: I will keep the minutes. Walk.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 16, dying memorial of Seongchung; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 384] A loyal servant does not forget his king even in death, so let me speak once before I die. I have always watched the shifting of the times, and war will surely come. In war one must choose the ground with care — only by meeting the enemy upstream can the country be preserved. If soldiers of another land should come, do not let them pass Chimhyeon by road, nor let their navy into the banks of Gibeolpo. Hold the difficult ground, and you may yet stop them.
The king does not take it in.
[QUOTE Stele of the Tang pacification of Baekje (扶餘 唐平百濟國碑), inscribed on the five-storey pagoda at Jeongnimsa; cited in Samguk Sagi bk. 28 n. on Uija yr. 16] Outwardly he cast off the ministers who spoke straight; inwardly he trusted strange women. Punishment fell only on the loyal and the good; favour and office went first to slanderers and flatterers.
Foxes in the Assembly. Toads in the treetops. A river running red. Nine signs, and a king who swears he doesn’t believe in signs…!

=== EPISODE 66: Nine Omens (659)
Around the kingdom, signs of Baekje’s impending doom gather.
Every one of them is real, in the sense that people saw it. That was always the only sense that mattered, and the man who said so is about to find out how much he meant it.
1. A herd of foxes infest the Ministers’ Assembly.
2. A hen mates with a sparrow.
3. A dead abnormally large fish washes up on the river.
4. A dead abnormally large woman washes up on the river.
5. The screams of ghosts can be heard from the palace.
6. The White River turns red with blood.
7. Tens of thousands of toads gathered in the tops of the trees.
8. Storm winds, rain, lightning. Black clouds like dragons fought each other in the air.
9. A ghost enters the palace and burrows into the ground. They dig, and find a turtle.
[FLASHBACK 659 A room in Surabol, some months earlier]
  chunchu: For twenty years Euija has been selling his people miracles. / Dragons. White deer.
  yushin: Knowing they were false?
  chunchu: He made them himself. / Which makes him the worst reader of signs alive. / He has spent his whole life knowing that signs are made by hands.
  yushin: …Then why would it work on him?
  chunchu: It doesn’t have to work on him. / It only has to work on his people.
  He does not order any of it, exactly. He asks for men who can travel, he asks what the markets of Sabi are frightened of, and he asks how deep one has to bury a turtle shell for the finding of it to look like an accident.
  chunchu: An army is the last thing you need to bring down a country. / First you need a rumour. / And you build a rumour out of what the people are already afraid of.
nation-baekje: Baekje falls! Baekje falls!
He keeps a shaman on retainer the way other kings keep song-girls. He likes watching someone else believe the sky talks; he has told Gyebek the gods are cheap civil servants, and told Gesomun the same with wine on his breath. The shaman thinks he is frightened. He lets her.
King Euija goes to a shaman with the nine signs piled behind him and the turtle in his hands. He wants the sky to say something he can still use.
euija: I came for amusement today. / There are nine. / Read them.
shaman: The foxes — the politicians are corrupt. / The hen and the sparrow — public morals have declined. / The great fish — the economy is in decline. / The great woman’s corpse — the people suffer for it.
shaman: The ghost-screams — the forgotten common man cries out. / The blood-red river — the public sphere is polluted. / The toads in the trees — only lying peddlers have loud voices. / The dragon-clouds — the nation begins fighting itself.
euija: …The turtle. / From the shell.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 20 (660); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 386] They obtained a tortoise; on its back was writing that said: Baekje is like the full moon; Silla is like the new moon.
shaman: To be like a full moon is to be full — and what is full must wane — / to be like a crescent is to be not yet full — and what is not yet full grows fuller. / Baekje wanes. Silla fills.
The blade is out before the last word cools. He cuts her down where she sits. The turtle’s sentence stays in the room.
euija: You wretch!!!
People start saying it out loud in the markets, which is how you know it is already over.
chunbok: Your Majesty. What you need right now is not wine.
chunbok: Your Majesty… / Say one name. / I will go and bring him.
euija: …That name was one I made up. / When I first took the throne.
chunbok: …Your Majesty.
euija: What are they saying in the markets these days.
chunbok: …That Baekje is the full moon.
euija: …Yes. / Well made.
He never says that the signs were made. He could name the price of every piece of it. To say a man made this one is to say it about the dragon over the Sabi, and the white deer, and the twenty years in between.
The best lie a man ever tells is the one he cannot afford to expose.
That night he leaves the palace the way he left it as a boy — without asking, without banners. The White River is waiting where it always waited. The omen said it ran red. Under the moon it is only black water and the smell of wet stone.
He has spent years drowning on dry land — wine, women, and refusing to hear the name of the man he sent away. The river does not care. It knew him before the crown.
euija: (to the water, and to a boy who once would have died on the twentieth dive) / I named you here. / I will not die drunk on the bank of my own invention.
He jumps. The cold takes the wine off him. When he surfaces he is coughing, furious, awake — the promising prince the eight clans once feared, scraped clean by the same river that taught him friendship.
euija: Summon Gyebek…!
Before the last stand, the first road. To understand Baekje, we have to go back to two brothers and their mother, walking south…!

=== EPISODE 67: Onjo (-18) [flashback]
Onjo and Biryu grow up princes in their father’s hall. Nobody there ever mentions Buyeo.
In Buyeo, Lady Ye has raised Jumong’s first son alone.
Yuri is a boy with a sling and bad aim, or good aim and bad luck. The pebble cracks a woman’s water jar on her way back from the well.
Water-carrier: Whose son are you, anyway? No father, no manners.
yuri: What kind of man was my father? Where is he now?
ladyye: Your father was no ordinary man, and the country could not hold him. So he fled to the southern land, founded a kingdom, and called himself king. When he left he said to me: “If you bear a son, tell him I left something hidden beneath the pine on the seven-sided stone. If he finds it, I will know him for my son.”
There is no pine on any hill he climbs. He finds it at home: the house’s pine pillar stands on a seven-sided foundation stone, and in the crack beneath it lies half a sword.
ladyye: Yuri….!
With his friends, three boys as stubborn as he is, he walks his father’s road backwards, south.
In the hall at Jolbon he lays the half-sword on the boards. Jumong goes to a chest nobody has opened since the river, takes out the other half, and kneels. The two halves click.
yuri: Father…!
Onjo and Biryu watch from the porch rail. The rail already knows what the hall will decide.
## The Last Night
When Yuri is named crown prince, Sosuno does not fight the hall. She packs the dusty-rose.
She packs Little Sosuno’s silence, which is not silent.
Jumong finds her at the old well, two buckets that have outlived the argument. Twenty winters in the same yard. He is still grinning. She is still pretending she came for water.
jumong: Hey. / You’re packed. / That’s… a lot of buckets for one road.
sosuno: Not buckets. / Grain. Boys. Me.
jumong: I left iron under a pine. I didn’t think it would grow up and walk in—
sosuno: Don’t— don’t make a speech. I’ll hit you.
jumong: Wasn’t going to. / Well’s still here. / I kept it. For you. Stupid, I know.
sosuno: Don’t be nice. / I’ll get stupid. / Yuri can have the chair. I’m not sitting in a footnote. / You know that. You always knew.
jumong: Yeah. / South, then. / Take the glow. Leave me the well. / …Come here. Please. One night. I’m still thirsty.
sosuno: Big idiot. / The boys are asleep. / If you compliment me I will scream. / …That’s not a no.
They do not make it to a feast. They make it to the grain room that has been theirs since the first night, and she kisses him before the door is shut.
Older. Hungrier. The hide has been off for years and she is worse now, not better.
jumong: Still you. / Still that mouth. / Look at you. Older. Sexier. Sorry. Not sorry.
sosuno: Don’t— ha— don’t say sexy I’ll— / Little Sosuno listen— that’s him— that’s the noise— wet— god the wet— twenty winters and still that slap— / Look at you. Chest. Back. That ass. That man meat. Still. Still. / Take it and destroy my tight little ass. Beat her up. Beat up Little Sosuno till she’s dripping and there’s nothing left—
jumong: Yours. / Always was. / Scream it. Last time. Louder.
sosuno: I hate you I love you don’t you dare stop— / Fill her— ruin her— she’s been waiting— / DUMB BIG IDIOT— LAST— FILL— / AHH— LITTLE SOSUNO’S— CUMMING— DON’T YOU LEAVE THE ROOM—
After, she is scarlet at what she heard herself say. Destroy. Beat her up. The whole book. He kisses the place on her temple that used to hide in a sleeve.
jumong: I heard. / You can still talk like that. / I’m keeping both of you. Even from a chair away.
Before dawn the lamp is out, and neither of them has slept.
sosuno: Don’t be nice. / I’ll get stupid. / …I’m already stupid. / Keep the well. I’m taking the glow.
jumong: Take it. / You’re beautiful. / Go found the other one. I’ll be here. Grinning. Like an idiot.
At dawn ten men start packing carts before anyone tells them to. Onjo and Biryu take their mother south. She walks like a woman who has been thoroughly answered and will not explain it to a deer, a son, or a chronicle. She carries the glow all the way south.
After wandering for a while they find a Heavenly Deer at what the older priests will call a heavenly door, a threshold between the yellow earth and the starred sky, and decide to settle there. Loyalty, they say later, is what you owe the door that let you in.
It happens like this. Three days south of the river, on a ridge path too narrow for the cart, a stag is standing in the way. Pale as mulberry paper, gold wherever the light touches it, antlers branching like a winter tree somebody decided to keep. It does not run. It looks at the three of them as if it had been told to expect three.
biryu: Don’t move. / That’s dinner for ten ministers. The antlers alone, a month of—
onjo: Hyung. Hyung, wait. / …That look like dinner to you? Really?
biryu: Looks like antlers to me. Meat with antlers.
sosuno: Biryu. Lower it. / …Listen to your mother. Bow down.
Biryu lowers the bow the way an elder son does, slowly enough that everyone understands it was his own idea. The stag turns, walks ten paces up the ridge, and stops to look back. When they do not follow, it waits. When they do, it walks on. It keeps that up for nine days.
onjo: It wants us to follow, right? / …A deer knows the way, Mother?
sosuno: Your father crossed a river on turtles’ backs. / A deer’s practically civilised.
On the ninth day it takes them up Mount Buak, and from the top the brothers see all of it: a river looped across the plain like a belt somebody has unbuckled, high peaks at their backs, wet green flats to the south and, somewhere past the haze, the sea. Biryu smells the salt before he sees it.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 23, Baekje Annals — King Onjo, founding; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1] At length they reached Hansan and climbed Mount Buak to look for land fit to live on. Biryu wished to live by the sea. The ten ministers remonstrated: “This land south of the river is belted by the Han to the north, held by high mountains to the east, looks out on fertile marshes to the south, and is barred by the great sea to the west. Such natural defences and advantages of ground are hard to come by. Would it not be fitting to make the capital here?” Biryu would not listen; he divided the people and went to Michuhol to live.
biryu: Smell that? Sea. I’m going there. / River in front, mountains behind, sure, lovely. You can’t float a ship on it.
onjo: Hyung, all ten of them say here. / …I mean, ten people can all be wrong, but all ten—
biryu: Then the ten can live here. / And Mother? Who’s Mother coming with?
sosuno: …Don’t ask me that.
Nobody answers him. The stag, which has stood a little apart all morning, crosses the summit and lies down in the grass at Onjo’s feet, facing the river. Biryu laughs too loudly and says the deer has no taste, and takes his half of the people down to Michuhol and the salt flats. The stag stays. Baekje will call it Sinrok, the guardian deer, for as long as Baekje has anything to call.
onjo: The land of ten tribes… Sipje! Hey, c’mon… we can think bigger than that. The land of a HUNDRED tribes… Baekje! Now that’s more like it….
onjo: “Baekje” — how does that sound?
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 23, Baekje Annals — King Onjo, founding; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 334] With ten ministers as wings he named the country Sipje. Later, because the common people had gladly followed at the time of coming, the name was changed to Baekje.
Back to Sabi. Two armies are already on the road, and the only plan anyone has is a dead man’s letter…!

=== EPISODE 68: Sungchung (660)
Word reaches Euija. Two armies are coming for his capital, one by sea and one over the hills. The markets already call it the Chunchu Army. He scrambles for troops.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 28, Baekje Annals — King Uija, yr. 16, dying memorial of Seongchung; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 384] If foreign troops come, do not let them pass Chimhyeon by land, and do not let their navy enter the shore of Gibeolpo; only then may it be done.
Loyalty, in Baekje, is a star you steer by after the door has already been opened against you.
In the Baekje court, there is panic as the Silla/Tang army is approaching the borders.
chunbok: Your Majesty, by Onjo’s shrine, we have too few troops to send General Gyebek! / Better to wait for Lord Satek’s men…
euija: Who is the Eraha of this country?! / Buyeo Euija? / Or Minister Satek? / Send him NOW!
At the back of the hall, the lord of Bear Fortress says nothing. Ye Sikjin is doing the sum every provincial lord is doing. How many days from the river mouth to the capital? And how many from the capital to his own gate?
One man might still know what to do. Euija sent him away too. Somebody ride. Now…!

=== EPISODE 69: Heungsu (660)
Heungsu is not in the hall. He is still at Gomamiji, where the posting put him. The king sends a man anyway, because the Chunchu Army is no longer a rumour and the rock has run out of plans.
[FLASHBACK 656 The berth]
  The last time the two of them spoke was at the water, before the paper named a county.
  heungsu: You… you truly mean to march? / With so few men—
  gyebek: I am a loyal servant of Baekje. / The king— / Our country has stood firm for seven hundred years.
  gyebek: His Majesty gave me a name. / A name — to a child who had none. / Today I go to give it back to him.
  heungsu: …Do you know the story of the Guardian of Ansi?
  gyebek: I do. / One person to cherish. One person to serve.
  gyebek: My trouble is that for me they are the same person.
  heungsu: Then hear one thing that is not a story. / Hold the White River mouth and the Tanhyeon pass — or there will be no Sabi left to be loyal to. / The Tang do not need our clans’ permission to land. They need our absence.
  gyebek: I know the roads. / Yellow Mountain first — if that door holds, the river still has a kingdom behind it. / If it does not… then the berths you all fought over will belong to whoever can spell our names.
[FLASHBACK 656–659 Gomamiji · 고마미지]
  The county is a day’s ride from the sea and a month from anyone who matters. Heungsu arrives with one chest and the office blade, hangs the blade on the doorpost by its ring, and on the first morning, before the clerk has finished his bow, scratches a map into the packed earth of the yard with the end of a broom handle.
  A coastline. One river mouth, the White River’s, drawn twice as wide as it is. One notch in the eastern hills for Tanhyeon. Sabi as a thumbprint. Every morning the chickens and the children walk it out of shape, and every morning he sweeps it flat and draws it again, the same lines in the same order, like a monk at his morning sutra.
  ?: Mister, is that a snake?
  heungsu: A river.
  ?: What river?
  heungsu: One I hope you never see.
  Nobody from Sabi writes. The news about Seongchung comes a season after the cell, on a salt boat, folded in between the price of salt and the price of rice, and the clerk reads it out because he reads everything out.
  ?: The councillor in Sabi. The one who— in the cell. / …Was he someone you knew, sir?
  heungsu: …Better handwriting than mine.
  That morning he does not draw the map. The next morning he does, and adds nothing to it, which the clerk takes as grief and the children take as permission to walk on Tanhyeon.
  In the last year the rumours come down the coast faster than the salt: foxes in the Ministers’ Assembly, a river gone red. Heungsu hears each one out and goes back to his broom.
The courier does not sit. Dust still on him. Heungsu’s ring is the first bright thing in the yard.
He has stopped in the middle of the yard, which is to say in the middle of the map.
?: His Majesty asks. / The matter is urgent. What then.
heungsu: …Seongchung already wrote it. / Same paper. I don’t have a second one.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Taejong Chunchu-gong — Uija asks the exile Heungsu] The matter is urgent — what then? He answered: It is generally the same as Jwapyeong Seongchung’s words.
?: …That is all? / His Majesty asked for a plan, sir. Not a—
heungsu: You’re standing on Tanhyeon.
The courier looks down and steps off a notch in the dirt, as if it might give way under him.
heungsu: Tell His Majesty— / …No. He has the paper.
The answer comes back to Sabi. The ministers do not like the source.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Taejong Chunchu-gong — ministers dismiss Heungsu; Uija agrees] Heungsu is bound; he resents his lord and has no love of country. His words must not be used. Better to let the Tang come down the White River without spreading their boats, and let Silla climb Tanhyeon by a path too narrow for horses abreast — then strike, and they will be as chickens in a basket, fish in a net. The king said: So it is.
euija: So it is.
The next courier is shorter. Tang keels are already in the mud of Gibeolpo. Yushin is already on the switchback. The White River and the Tanhyeon pass are already theirs.
No second courier comes to Gomamiji. Heungsu sweeps the yard and draws the map for eleven more mornings, the river mouth still twice as wide as it is, because nobody has told him it is already full of Tang keels.
On the twelfth it rains, and he stands under the eave and watches the White River and Tanhyeon run together into one brown puddle. He does not draw them again. He lifts the blade off the doorpost by its ring and starts north on foot, toward a pass that has already been crossed.
The histories do not mention him again.
Across the sea, a boat is coming for the Turtle. He is on the shore before they finish tying it up…!

=== EPISODE 70: Gyebek (660)
Somewhere in the fourth year he notices he has stopped counting the days. It frightens him for a week. Then it does not.
He stops correcting the people who call him Turtle, and carries water for the women who dive. For the first and last time in his life, he is in a place where being exactly what he is costs him nothing.
A boat comes for him in the fifth year. He is on the shore before they finish tying it up.
yuridora: Turtle. What is the hurry. / You could die comfortable here.
gyebek: Nothing here is mine to keep.
yuridora: Then what is yours.
gyebek: …A promise.
He takes nothing off the island except the stories, which is the only export it has ever had.
yuridora: Turtle. Learn one thing before you go. / A story is not begun with its ending already fixed.
gyebek: …Mine is fixed.
Five years of listening, and that is the one lesson that does not take.
You can teach a man every story on the island. You cannot make him believe he is inside one.
He says goodbye at the water. It takes longer than he planned.
yuridora: Gyebek! It gladdened me to know a man like you. / Once you go back to the mainland, who knows if we shall meet again. / Promise me just one thing. / Do not forget people.
gyebek: …My lord. / I am a man with no name—
gyebek: …My lord. I was a child with no family and no name. / And then the crown prince of a kingdom took me in, raised me, and trusted me. / Such a debt— / I am an ignorant man who cannot even read. / But as a man, I will keep faith.
Before he marches he goes home. What he does there he does so that nothing of his can be used against him, and the histories record it in one line.
He comes out before the light is properly up. The yard is swept. Nothing in it is his any more except a black horse at the post. Gomanari is named for the bear ferry where Gyebek learned to ride. It is the one thing he owns that the Tang cannot sell in a slave market.
The groom, a boy from the next village who did not sleep in the house and is therefore alive, holds the bridle out at arm’s length and will not look at him.
?: H-here, General. / …Gomanari too?
gyebek: A horse can’t be made a slave. / A horse is just a horse.
He saddles it himself, counting the buckles under his breath, and when he is done he stands with his forehead against the black neck for exactly as long as it takes to count to ten. Then he mounts and does not look at the house.
Gyebek and his five thousand set out for the Yellow Mountain. It is the last latch on the road to Sabi. Merchants have cursed its summer dust for years.
gyebek: Long live Baekje….!
Five thousand march for the Yellow Mountain. High above them, in a pavilion made of clouds, someone has called a meeting…!
